label: native
etymology_text:
Inherited from Proto-South Dravidian *ñān.
Cognates
Cognate with Irula நா (nā), Old Kannada ನಾನ್ (nān), Kannada ನಾನು (nānu), Malayalam ഞാൻ (ñāṉ) and Telugu నా (nā), నేను (nēnu).
Unrelated to Proto-Dravidian *yĀn, whose descendant is யான் (yāṉ). However, the oblique forms of this pronoun are suppleted from யான் (yāṉ). Compare the similar case of suppletion in நாங்கள் (nāṅkaḷ).

Cognate with Kannada ಎಲೆ (ele), Old Kannada ಎಲೆ (ele), Tulu ಇರೆ (ire)/Tulu ಇಲೆ (ile), Malayalam ഇല (ila), Kodava [script needed] (elakaṇḍa), Toda [script needed] (es̱), Kota (India) [script needed] (el).

label: native

False cognate of Japanese いる (iru).

label: native

Cognate with Badaga நீரு (nīru), Brahui دیر (dīr), Kannada ನೀರು (nīru), Malayalam നീര് (nīrŭ), Telugu నీరు (nīru), Toda நீர் (nīr), Tulu ನೀರ್ (nīrŭ).

Cognate with Malayalam കിഴക്ക് (kiḻakkŭ).

label: native

label: native

etymology_text: From Proto-Indo-Aryan *śćand-, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *śćand-, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ḱend-.

etymology_text: From Proto-Indo-European *ǵews- (“to taste, try”). Cognates include Latin gustus, Persian دوست (dust, “friend”), Old English ċēosan (whence English choose).

etymology_text: Inherited from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂- (“to protect”); Cognate with Old Persian 𐎱𐎠𐎮𐎹 (pādiy), Latin pascō (“to feed, maintain”), Mycenaean Greek 𐀡𐀕 (po-me). Probably not related to पाल (pāla, “guard”), despite popular folk etymology; see there for more.

etymology_text: From Proto-Indo-European *preḱ- (“to ask”). Cognate with Russian (во)прос ((vo)pros, “question”), Latin prex whence, via French, English pray.

etymology_text: From Proto-Indo-European *pleth₂- (“flat”). Cognates include Ancient Greek πλᾰτῠ́ς (plătŭ́s, “flat, broad”) whence ultimately place, plaza, plate, platter, plateau; Lithuanian plėsti (“to expand”); Proto-Slavic *pleťè (“shoulder”); English flat, fold, field.

etymology_text: From Proto-Indo-European *bʰreh₁ǵ- (“to shine”). Cognate with Avestan 𐬠𐬭𐬁𐬰𐬀𐬌𐬙𐬌 (brāzaⁱti), Persian برازیدن (barâzidan), Lithuanian brė́kšti, Proto-Slavic *brězgъ (“dawn”), Albanian bardhë, English bright, Welsh berth.

etymology_text: From Proto-Indo-Iranian *maržd- (“to forgive, spare, to pity”), possibly an extension of *marš- (“to forget”), whence मृष् (mṛṣ).

label: native
etymology_text: Probably from Proto-Indo-European *(H)melḱ-. Cognate with Latin mulceō (“to stroke, touch lightly”).

label: native

Noun sense 1 is a semantic loan from French amateur.

label: native
etymology_text: From Old Galician-Portuguese pavio, from Vulgar Latin *papīlum, from Latin papȳrus. Doublet of papiro.

label: native
etymology_text: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese sẽo, from Latin sinus. Ultimately of Proto-Indo-European origin. Doublet of seno and sino. Cognate with Galician seo, Spanish seno, and French sein.

label: native
etymology_text: From Old Galician-Portuguese trõar, from Latin tonāre (with an -r- due to influence from Latin tonitrus, Vulgar Latin *tronitus; see also estrondo and trom), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tenh₂- (“to thunder”). Compare Catalan and Spanish tronar.

label: native
etymology_text: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese salmoira, from Late Latin salimuria, from Latin sal + muria.

label: native
etymology_text: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese alen, from Latin ad + illinc (“thence, there”).

label: native
etymology_text:
From Old Galician-Portuguese façanna, from Old Spanish fazaña, of disputed origin. Suggested derivations include:
* Andalusian Arabic حَسَنَة (ḥasana) with influence of facer (“to do”), from Arabic حَسَنَة (ḥasana, “good deed”)
* from a form of facer (“to do”), specifically:
** Old Spanish faciana
** Vulgar Latin *facinus
** Vulgar Latin *facianea, reportedly attested as fazania

label: native
etymology_text: From Latin vitta (“ribbon”).

label: English
etymology_text: From English Virginia, from Latin Virginia.

label: native
etymology_text: Inherited from Latin planarius (“planar”).

label: Arabic
etymology_text: From Arabic اَلْوَزِير (al-wazīr, “minister, vizier”). Doublet of vizir.

label: native
etymology_text: From Old Galician-Portuguese pousada, from pousar (“to rest”) + -ada, from Latin pausāre (“to halt”).

label: native
etymology_text: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese alçar, from Vulgar Latin *altiāre, derived from Latin altus (“high”). Compare Galician and Spanish alzar

label: native
etymology_text: From Old Galician-Portuguese corõar, from Latin corōnāre (“to crown”); compare Catalan and Spanish coronar.

label: native
etymology_text: From Old Galician-Portuguese tẽem, from Latin tenent. Cognate with Galician teñen and Spanish tienen. Also compare with vêm.

label: native
etymology_text: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese crecer, from Latin crēscere (“to grow”), from Proto-Italic *krēskō, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱreh₁- (“to grow, become bigger”).

label: Hindi
etymology_text: Borrowed from English cheetah, from Hindi चीता (cītā, “leopard, panther”), ultimately from Sanskrit चित्र (citra, “multicolored, speckled”).

label: Hindi
etymology_text: Borrowed from Hindi छींट (chī̃ṭ).

label: native
etymology_text: From Old Galician-Portuguese sequer, siquer, corresponding to se (“if”) + quer (“(one) wants”). Cognate with Spanish siquiera.

label: Arabic
etymology_text: Borrowed from Arabic مَطْمُورَة (maṭmūra).

label: native
etymology_text:
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese Castro, from castro (“fortification”). Cognate with Galician and Spanish Castro.
The municipality in Brazil was named after Portuguese minister Martinho de Melo e Castro.

label: native
etymology_text: From Old Galician-Portuguese poupar, from Latin palpāre (“to touch softly”). Doublet of the borrowing palpar and apalpar.

label: native
etymology_text: From Old Galician-Portuguese capela (“chapel”), from Medieval Latin, Late Latin cappella (“little cloak; chapel”), diminutive of cappa (“cloak, cape”). Cognate with Galician capela, Spanish capilla, Catalan capella, Occitan capèla, French chapelle, Italian cappella and Romanian capelă.

label: native
etymology_text: Either imitative or inherited from Vulgar Latin *verrāre, from verrēs (“boar”). Compare Spanish berrear and Romanian zbiera.

label: native
etymology_text: Borrowed from Galician serao, sarao, from Old Galician-Portuguese serão, from Vulgar Latin *seranum, from Latin sērus (“late”). Doublet of serão.

label: native
etymology_text: From Old Galician-Portuguese sar, saar, sãar, influenced by Old Portuguese çarrar (Modern cerrar), from Latin sanāre. Doublet of sanar.

label: native
etymology_text: From Old Galician-Portuguese adevinnar, adevỹar, from Latin ad + dīvīnāre (“foretell”).

label: native
etymology_text: Inherited from Latin mēta (“cone, pyramid; boundary limit”).

label: native
etymology_text: From fole + -ar, ultimately from Latin follis.

label: native
etymology_text:
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese prazer, a semi-learned borrowing from Latin placēre. Compare Spanish placer and Galician pracer.
(interjection): Ellipsis of phrases such as é um prazer conhecê-lo/la (“it’s a pleasure to meet you”).

label: native
etymology_text: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese qual quer, from qual + quer. By surface analysis, qual (“which one”) + quer (“wants”). Compare Galician calquera, Spanish cualquiera, and Italian (literary) qualsivoglia.

label: native
etymology_text: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese donaire, borrowed from Old Spanish donaire, from Late Latin dōnārius, from Latin dōnārium.

label: Persian
etymology_text: Borrowed from Persian مغول (moġul), an Arabic and Persian corruption of Mongol, ultimately from Middle Mongol ᠮᠣᠩᠭᠣᠯ (mongɣol). Doublet of mongol.

label: native
etymology_text: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese [Term?], from Old Occitan ambaisador (“ambassador”), derivative of ambaissa (“service, mission, errand”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *ambahtaz (“servant”), from Gaulish ambaxtos (“servant”).

label: native
etymology_text: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese vassalo, from Medieval Latin vassallus (“manservant, domestic, retainer”), from vassus (“servant”), from Gaulish *wassos (“young man, squire”), from Proto-Celtic *wastos (“servant”) (compare Old Irish foss and Welsh gwas).

label: native
etymology_text: From Latin taxus, from Scythian. Compare Galician teixo, Asturian texu, and Spanish tejo.

label: native
etymology_text: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese roupa, from Gothic *𐍂𐌰𐌿𐍀𐌰 (*raupa), from 𐍂𐌰𐌿𐍀𐌾𐌰𐌽 (raupjan). Cognate with Spanish ropa. See also Portuguese roubar.

label: native
etymology_text: From Old Galician-Portuguese soomente~soamente, from Early Medieval Latin sōlā mente. By surface analysis, só + -mente.

label: native
etymology_text: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese conselho, from Latin cōnsilium. Doublet of consílio, a borrowing. Compare Galician consello.

label: native
etymology_text: From Old Galician-Portuguese quan, from Latin quam.

label: native
etymology_text: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese afastar, of obscure origin; maybe from Proto-Germanic *fastuz (“fixed, firm”), through Suevic [Term?] or Gothic.

label: Arabic
etymology_text: From Arabic كفتة (kufta), from Persian کوفته (kufte, “ground meat”).

label: English
etymology_text: Unadapted borrowing from English post-it, a trademark genericization, from the brand name post-it.

label: native
etymology_text: Old Galician-Portuguese vẽen, from Latin veniunt. Cognate with Galician veñen and Spanish vienen. Also compare with têm.

label: native
etymology_text: From Vulgar Latin *involtus, from *involvitus or *involŭtus, for Latin involūtus. Doublet of involuto.

label: native
etymology_text: From Old Galician-Portuguese pichel (13th century, Cantigas de Santa Maria), from Old French pichier (“small jug”), from Late Latin pīcārium, alteration of bīcārium, itself possibly from bacarium, bacar or from Ancient Greek βῖκος (bîkos). Compare English pitcher; more at beaker.

label: English
etymology_text: First recorded in Brazil in the 1980s. Rendering of English Michael, having become popular due to Michael Jackson’s fame. The ending ⟨-on⟩ may be due to the nasalization of the original final diphthong /ow/ > [õw̃]. Doublet of Miguel.

label: native
etymology_text: Inherited from Latin sporadicus, borrowed from Ancient Greek σποραδικός (sporadikós).

label: Arabic
etymology_text: Borrowed from Arabic زَرْبَطَانَة (zarbaṭāna, “blowgun”).

label: native
etymology_text: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese carreira, from Early Medieval Latin via carrāria, from Latin carrus, from Gaulish *karros, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱr̥sós, from *ḱers- (“to run”).. Compare Galician carreira and Spanish carrera. Cognate with also English career. By surface analysis, carro + -eira.

label: native
etymology_text: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese ponho, from Latin pōnō.

label: Arabic
etymology_text: From colloquial Arabic اَلزَّغَايَة (az-zaḡāya), from Proto-Berber *zaġāya (“spear”).

label: native
etymology_text: Feminine diminutive of machado (“axe”), from Latin masclus (“male”), earlier masculus, diminutive of mās (“man”).

label: native
etymology_text: From Vulgar Latin *macla, from Latin macula (“stain”). Compare the doublets mancha, malha, mácula, mágoa, and mangra.

label: native
etymology_text: Inherited from Late Latin coriācea (vestis), from coriāceus, from Latin corium. Compare French cuirasse, source of English cuirass.

label: Arabic
etymology_text: Borrowed from Arabic مَمْلُوك (mamlūk, “slave”).

label: native
etymology_text: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese caravela, a diminutive of cáravo, or cárabo, from Ancient Greek κᾱ́ραβος (kā́rabos, “light ship, horned beetle”).

label: Arabic
etymology_text: Ultimately from Arabic حِنَّاء (ḥinnāʔ). Doublet of henê.

label: native
etymology_text: From Vulgar Latin *incalciāre, derived from Latin calx (“heel”).

label: native
etymology_text: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese aquele, from Vulgar Latin *eccum ille, from Latin eccum + ille. Cognate with Spanish aquel.

label: native
etymology_text: From Old Galician-Portuguese [Term?], from Latin trāns (“across, beyond”), from Proto-Indo-European *terh₂- (“through, throughout, over”). Doublet of trans- and trans.

label: native
etymology_text: From Old Galician-Portuguese terreiro, from Late Latin terrārius, from Latin terra. By surface analysis, terra + -eiro.

label: native
etymology_text: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese misson, mison, from Latin missiōnem.

label: native
etymology_text: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese traiçon, from Latin trāditiōnem (“a giving up, handing over, surrender, delivery, tradition”), from trādō (“give up, hand over, deliver over, betray”, verb), from trāns- (“over, across”) + dō (“give”) (from Proto-Indo-European *deh₃- (“to give”)). By surface analysis, trair + -ção. Doublet of tradição. Cognate with Galician traizón, Spanish traición, French t

label: native
etymology_text: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese praga (“sore, curse”), borrowed from Latin plāga (“wound, misfortune”). Compare the inherited chaga.

label: native
etymology_text: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese ves, from Latin vidēs. Cognate with Galician ves and Spanish ves. Compare crês and lês.

label: native
etymology_text: From Vulgar Latin *mancipius (“slave”), from Latin mancipium (“purchase property”), also "a bought slave". For sense "coatrack" compare English valet.

label: native
etymology_text:
From Old Galician-Portuguese yrto, from Vulgar Latin *erctus, vernacular variant of Classical Latin ērēctus, therefore a doublet of ereto.
Despite the resemblance, unlikely to derive from Latin hirtus (“shaggy”). Compare Galician irto, Spanish yerto.

label: native
etymology_text: From Old Galician-Portuguese descarregar, from Late Latin discarricāre (“to unload”), from carricō (“to load”), from Latin carrus (“car, wagon”). By surface analysis, des- + carregar.

label: Arabic
etymology_text: Perhaps onomatopoeic, related to alalá, or from Arabic عَرِيض (ʕarīḍ).

label: native
etymology_text: Inherited from Latin cervārius (“pertaining to a stag”), from cervus (“deer, stag”). Doublet of serval.

label: English
etymology_text: From English systemic or sistema + -ico.

label: native
etymology_text: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese chus, from Latin plūs (“more”). Displaced by collateral mais.

label: native
etymology_text: From Vulgar Latin *disdignāre, reshaping of Latin dēdignārī (“disdain, scorn”) from dignārī. Compare Spanish desdeñar, Italian disdegnare, French dédaigner.

label: native
etymology_text: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese fidalgo, shortened from fillo d'algo (literally “son of something”), meaning "person of property/wealth". Compare Spanish hidalgo (Old Spanish fidalgo).

label: native
etymology_text: From Old Galician-Portuguese loucura, from louco (“crazy”). By surface analysis, louco + -ura.

label: native
etymology_text: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese laço, from Vulgar Latin *laceus, from Latin laqueus (“noose; snare”).

label: Arabic
etymology_text: Borrowed from Early Modern Spanish ojalá, from Arabic وَشَاءَ ٱلله (wašāʔa llāh, “and may God will it”) or لَوْ شَاءَ ٱلله (law šāʔa llāh, “if God wills it”). Compare English inshallah.

label: native
etymology_text: From Vulgar Latin *combattere, from Latin cum + battuō.

label: native
etymology_text: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *sorum, from Latin serum. Doublet of sérum.

label: native
etymology_text: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese -dade, from Latin -tātem, from Proto-Indo-European *-teh₂ts.

label: native
etymology_text: From Old Galician-Portuguese -avel, from Latin -ābilis. Compare -able dialectally and in various other languages; e.g. Sicilian -àvili, for a similar morphology.

label: native
etymology_text: From Old Galician-Portuguese queixada (“jaw”), from Vulgar Latin *capseāta, a derivative of Vulgar Latin *capseus (“chin”) (whence queixo), itself a derivative of Latin capsa (“box”), from capiō (“capture, seize, take”), from Proto-Indo-European *kap- (“to take, seize, catch, grasp”). By surface analysis, queixo + -ada.

label: native
etymology_text: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese raia (“ray”), from Latin raia (“ray”), of uncertain origin.

label: native
etymology_text: Uncertain. Likely from raio (“beam”) + -a (forms feminine equivalents), or from an equivalent Vulgar Latin *radia, ultimately from Latin radius. Cognates include Galician raia and Spanish raya.

label: native
etymology_text: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese alfaia, from Arabic الحَاجَة (al-ḥāja, “necessary thing; valuable thing”). Compare Galician alfaia and Spanish alhaja.

label: native
etymology_text: Inherited from Latin appendere (“to hang”), from ap- + pendō (“to hang”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)pend- (“to pull; to spin”).

label: native
etymology_text: From Old Galician-Portuguese apelido, from Latin appellitō (“to be accustomed to call”), from appellō (“to address”).

label: native
etymology_text: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese deitar, from a Vulgar Latin *dēctāre, from Latin dējectāre, frequentative of dējicere (“to throw, hurl down”).

label: native
etymology_text: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese lavra, from Latin labōra (“toil”).

label: native
etymology_text: From Old Galician-Portuguese pucaro, from Latin poculum, from Proto-Italic *pōtlo- (with the instrument suffix *-tlo-, that yields -culum, compare Sanskrit पात्र (pātra, “drinking vessel”)), from Proto-Indo-European *peh₃- (“drink”). Compare bibo.

label: native
etymology_text: From Old Galician-Portuguese mercar (“to trade; to buy”), from Vulgar Latin *mercāre, from Latin mercārī (“to trade”), from merx (“merchandise”), possibly from Etruscan [Term?].

label: native
etymology_text: From Old Galician-Portuguese cabron (cabra + -on (augmentative suffix)). Compare Spanish cabrón, Catalan cabró, Italian caprone, Venetan cavron. By surface analysis, cabra + -ão

label: native
etymology_text: Probably inherited from Latin saniēs, Late Latin sania interpreted as the base of īnsānia (“unsoundness of mind”).

label: native
etymology_text: From Old Galician-Portuguese tallar, from Late Latin tāliāre, from Latin tālea. Compare French tailler, Italian tagliare, Romanian tăia, Spanish tajar.

label: Arabic
etymology_text: From Latin baiulāre (“to carry a burden”) or perhaps from Arabic بَجُلَ (bajula, “to be worshipped”).

label: native
etymology_text: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese cortes (“courtly”), from corte (“court”) + -es.

label: native
etymology_text: From Old Galician-Portuguese ouvydo (displacing collateral form oydo), from earlier *ouido, from Latin audītus.

label: native
etymology_text: From Old Galician-Portuguese tamanno, from Latin tam magnus.

label: native
etymology_text: From Old Galician-Portuguese coberto, from Latin coopertus, perfect passive participle of cooperiō (“to cover wholly”). Compare Galician cuberto.

label: native
etymology_text: From Latin legis. Cognate with Galician les and Spanish lees. Compare crês and vês.

label: Arabic
etymology_text: Borrowed from Arabic أَبُو سِمْبَل (ʔabū simbal).

label: native
etymology_text: From Old Galician-Portuguese estender, from Latin extendere.

label: native
etymology_text: From Old Galician-Portuguese louvar, from earlier louar, loar, from Latin laudāre (“to praise”), from laus (“praise”). Piecewise doublet of laudar.

label: native
etymology_text: From Old Galician-Portuguese Ruben, from Latin Ruben, from Hebrew רְאוּבֵן.

label: native
etymology_text: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese rebentar, possibly from Vulgar Latin *repentāre, from Latin repēns (“sudden, unexpected”).

label: native
etymology_text: From Old Galician-Portuguese maciço, from Vulgar Latin *massīcius. By surface analysis, massa + -iço. Compare Spanish macizo. Doublet of massivo.

label: native
etymology_text: From chuva (“rain”) + -oso or from Latin pluviōsus. Compare Galician chuvioso, Spanish lluvioso. Compare the borrowed doublet pluvioso.

label: native
etymology_text: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese ravioso, with metathesis, from Latin rabiōsus. By surface analysis, raiva + -oso. Compare Galician rabioso.

label: native
etymology_text: From Old Galician-Portuguese estavel, from Latin stabilis. By surface analysis, estar + -ável.

label: native
etymology_text: From Old Galician-Portuguese caldeyra, from Late Latin caldāria~caldārium (“cooking-pot”), derived from Latin caldus (“hot”). Doublet of caldeiro.

label: native
etymology_text: From Old Galician-Portuguese redor, from Latin retrō (“backwards; behind”, adverb). Doublet of retrô.

label: Arabic
etymology_text: Borrowed from Spanish nácar, ultimately from Arabic نَقَّارَة (naqqāra, “small drum”).

label: Arabic
etymology_text: From Arabic شِيعَة (šīʕa, “Shia”) + -ita.

label: native
etymology_text: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese perdõar (“to forgive”), from Late Latin perdōnāre.

label: native
etymology_text: From Old Galician-Portuguese esforçado, past participle of esforçar.

label: native
etymology_text: From Old Galician-Portuguese chopo, from Vulgar Latin *ploppus, from a metathetical alteration and contraction of Classical Latin pōpulus (“poplar”). Compare Spanish chopo.

label: native
etymology_text: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese escorregar, from Vulgar Latin *excurricāre.

label: native
etymology_text: From Old Galician-Portuguese crueldade, from Latin crūdēlitātem.

label: native
etymology_text: From Old Galician-Portuguese -ela, from Latin -ella.

label: English
etymology_text: From English to tune (“to adjust a mechanical, electric or electronic device”).

label: native
etymology_text: From Old Galician-Portuguese Evora, from Latin Ebora, a feminine noun derived from Proto-Celtic *eburos (“yew”).

label: native
etymology_text: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese Guimarães, from Early Medieval Latin [Vīlla] Vīmarānem. Cognate with Galician Guimarans and Guimaréns.

label: native
etymology_text: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese Odimira. Analyzed as Ode-, from Arabic وَادٍ (wādin, “river”), + Mira.

label: native
etymology_text: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese Santaren, after Visigothic saint Santa Irene.

label: native
etymology_text: From Old Galician-Portuguese Silve, from Latin Cilpe.

label: Arabic
etymology_text: A mix of the Arabic name of the city, القَصْر أَبِي دَانِس (al-qaṣr ʔabī dānis), and the Latin name of the city, Salacia.

label: native
etymology_text: From Old Galician-Portuguese Almadã, from Arabic المَعْدِن (al-maʕdin, literally “the mine”).

label: Arabic
etymology_text: Borrowed from Arabic الْمَائِدَة (al-māʔida, “the plateau”).

label: Arabic
etymology_text: Borrowed from Arabic الْمُدَوَّر (al-mudawwar, “the round thing”). The name probably refers to a nearby hill; تَلّ اَلْمُدَوَّر (tall al-mudawwar, “round hill”) is a fairly common Arabic placename.

label: Arabic
etymology_text: Borrowed from Arabic بَيَّاز (bayyāz, “falconer”).

label: native
etymology_text: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese Amarante, from Early Medieval Latin [Villa] Amaranthi (“Amarantus' villa”). Compare Galician Amarante.

label: native
etymology_text: From Late Latin campānia (“open country, battlefield”), from campāneus, from Latin campus (“field”). Compare Spanish campaña, Italian campagna, French champagne. Doublet of champanhe, borrowed from French.

label: native
etymology_text: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese aleive, from Arabic العَيْب (al-ʕayb). Cognate with Spanish aleve.

label: native
etymology_text: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese Belmonte, blend of belo (“beautiful”) + monte (“hill”).

label: native
etymology_text: From Old Galician-Portuguese Braga, from Latin Bracara Augusta, named after a Celtic tribe, the Bracari. Doublet of Brácara.

label: native
etymology_text: From Latin Brigantia, from Proto-Celtic *Brigantī, *brigantī, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰérǵʰonts (“high”), from the root *bʰerǵʰ- (“to rise”) + *-onts (adjective-forming suffix).

label: native
etymology_text:
From Old Galician-Portuguese badalo (“bell-clapper”), from Vulgar Latin *batāclum, from contraction of *ba(t)tuāculum, from Latin battuere (“to beat, to clap”).
Cognate with Galician badal, Spanish badajo, Catalan batall, French batail, Italian batacchio.

label: native
etymology_text: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese acender, from Latin accendere (“to kindle or light a fire”).

label: native
etymology_text: From Old Galician-Portuguese açor, from Latin accipiter (“hawk”).

label: native
etymology_text: From Old Galician-Portuguese abalar, from Vulgar Latin *advallāre, probably ultimately from Latin vallis (“vale, valley”).

label: native
etymology_text: From Old Galician-Portuguese mecer, from Latin miscēre (“to mix”). Compare Spanish mecer.

label: native
etymology_text: Inherited from Latin [Aquae] Flāviae (“Flavian Waters/Thermae”), from Flāvius (“Flavian gens”, adjective). Doublet of flávio.

label: native
etymology_text: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese Coimbra, from Latin Conimbriga (“Condeixa-a-Velha”), with the first element possibly being named after the Conii people, and the second element from Proto-Celtic *brigā. Doublet of Conímbriga.

label: native
etymology_text: From Old Galician-Portuguese Halaf, Falaf, from Arabic [Term?] (“Jalaf”).
